General.Description:
On the morning of her forty-third birthday, Marta Velde begins to hear tomorrow's sounds. Not visions — not prophecy — just sound. The conversation she will have at breakfast tomorrow, arriving in her ears today, twelve hours early. The phone call she has not yet received. The music playing in a room she will not enter until the following afternoon.

The condition is not painful. It is not, at first, frightening. It is simply, in a word Marta returns to throughout the novel, strange.

Echoes of Tomorrow is a literary speculative fiction novel that uses its central premise with precise restraint — this is not a time travel story, and Marta cannot change what she hears. She can only hear it, earlier than she was supposed to, and decide what to do with the knowledge. Vera Landin is interested in what it means to live in time, and what grief does to our experience of before and after, when the person we expected to share our future is no longer there.

The novel is structured so that its two timelines — Marta's present and the sounds of her future — gradually and heartbreakingly converge. The technical achievement is considerable. The emotional achievement is larger.

One of the most affecting novels in recent memory.
